title: King Afonso Protests to the King of Portugal
text:
Afonso I, called Nzinga Mbemba before his baptism, ruled the Kingdom of Kongo in west central Africa from about 1509 to the early 1540s. He was a Christian, literate in Portuguese, and an ally of Portugal. He welcomed Portuguese priests, teachers and craftsmen, sent young Kongolese nobles to study in Lisbon, and traded with Portuguese merchants.

That trade increasingly meant slaves. In 1526 Afonso wrote several letters to King Joao III of Portugal, which survive in the Portuguese archives. He complained that Portuguese merchants were flooding his kingdom with goods, encouraging his own subjects to defy him, and seizing free people, even nobles and members of the royal family, to sell them overseas. He wrote that the country was being depopulated. He asked the Portuguese king to send no more merchants or goods, only priests and teachers and what was needed for the church.

Afonso then set up a commission of officials to inspect every captive before export and to free anyone who had been taken illegally. He did not end the trade, which he too took part in under those rules, and Portugal ignored his request to stop it.
lesson: A leader must be willing to name a harm that enriches powerful people around him, even when he cannot stop it alone.
people: Afonso I of Kongo (Nzinga Mbemba), Joao III of Portugal
location: Mbanza Kongo, Kingdom of Kongo (modern Angola)
source: Letters of Afonso I to Joao III, 1526, Portuguese archives (published in Antonio Brasio, Monumenta Missionaria Africana)
